note: Interactions are matched either by substance id or by the tags a substance carries (see tags.json). Severity: danger > caution > note.

interactions.title: Opioid + sedative: respiratory depression is more than additive
interactions.text: Opioids suppress the brainstem's response to carbon dioxide; benzodiazepines, alcohol and gabapentinoids suppress arousal and airway tone. Together the effect is synergistic, not additive — doses that each would be survivable alone combine into respiratory arrest. The majority of opioid-related deaths involve a second depressant, and benzodiazepines are the most common one. Overlap on the timeline is the thing to look at: the danger is greatest where both curves are high at once.
interactions.what_to_do: If both are present anyway: space them far apart rather than together, reduce both substantially, never use alone, and keep naloxone to hand — though naloxone reverses only the opioid, not the sedative.

interactions.title: Opioid + alcohol: the most common fatal combination
interactions.text: Alcohol adds respiratory depression, suppresses the gag reflex and causes vomiting — so an opioid dose that would have been survivable becomes an aspiration or respiratory arrest. Alcohol's own curve is slow and long, so the overlap window is wide.
interactions.what_to_do: Separate them by many hours if at all. Someone unconscious with both on board must be in the recovery position and not left alone.

interactions.title: Sedative + alcohol: deep sedation and lost airway reflexes
interactions.text: Benzodiazepines and alcohol act on overlapping sites of the same GABA-A receptor. Alone, benzodiazepines have a relatively high ceiling for respiratory depression; with alcohol that ceiling disappears. Anterograde amnesia is also far more likely, so people act without forming memories.
interactions.what_to_do: Avoid the combination. If it has happened, the risks are airway and falls — position them on their side and stay.

interactions.title: GHB + alcohol: overlapping metabolism and additive sedation
interactions.text: Both are cleared by saturable routes that compete, and both are potent CNS depressants. GHB's dose-response is already extremely steep; adding alcohol shifts the point of unconsciousness to a much lower GHB dose and makes vomiting while unresponsive likely. This combination is responsible for a large share of GHB deaths.
interactions.what_to_do: This is the single combination most worth avoiding outright. There is no antidote for GHB; the whole intervention is airway management.

interactions.title: Cocaine + alcohol: your liver makes a third drug
interactions.text: Together they form cocaethylene, which exists only when both are present. It is roughly as psychoactive as cocaine but with a half-life around three times longer, and it is more cardiotoxic — it carries a higher risk of sudden cardiac death than either substance alone. It also means cardiac strain continues long after the cocaine itself has gone.
interactions.what_to_do: The risk is cardiac and it outlasts the evening. Chest pain in this context is an emergency.

interactions.title: Stimulant + depressant: each hides the other
interactions.text: A stimulant masks how sedated you are, so people keep taking the depressant; when the stimulant clears first — and it usually does, since cocaine's half-life is about an hour — the full depressant load arrives at once with nothing opposing it. The cardiovascular system meanwhile gets opposing instructions simultaneously.
interactions.what_to_do: Watch the two curves on the timeline: the dangerous moment is where the stimulant falls away while the depressant is still high.

interactions.title: Cocaine + opioid: mismatched timecourses
interactions.text: Cocaine's half-life is about an hour; most opioids last several. The stimulant masks the opioid's sedation while it is present, and respiratory depression arrives when it goes. Taking more opioid while the cocaine is up is how people end up far deeper than intended.
interactions.what_to_do: The overlap on the timeline shows it: the risk window opens as the cocaine curve drops, not while it is high.

interactions.title: MDMA + SSRI: blunted effect, and a serotonin syndrome risk
interactions.text: An SSRI occupies the serotonin transporter that MDMA needs in order to work, so the effect is substantially reduced — which reliably leads to redosing, and redosing MDMA raises exposure disproportionately because it inhibits its own clearance. Meanwhile both raise synaptic serotonin, so the combination carries serotonin syndrome risk. Fluoxetine's active metabolite persists for weeks, so stopping it recently does not remove the interaction.
interactions.what_to_do: The blunting is not something to overcome with more. Fluoxetine in particular needs about five weeks to clear.

interactions.title: Serotonin syndrome risk
interactions.text: Two serotonergic drugs together can produce serotonin syndrome: agitation, rigidity, tremor, and a rising temperature that can become fatal. Hyperthermia is already MDMA's main acute danger, and this compounds it. MAOIs are the most dangerous partner — including the harmala alkaloids in ayahuasca preparations — but tramadol, SSRIs and triptans all contribute.
interactions.what_to_do: Rising temperature, rigidity and confusion together are a medical emergency, not a bad trip.

interactions.title: SSRI + codeine: the painkiller stops working
interactions.text: Codeine only relieves pain because CYP2D6 converts it to morphine. Fluoxetine and paroxetine are potent CYP2D6 inhibitors, so they turn a normal metabolizer into a functional poor metabolizer — the codeine still causes nausea and constipation, but produces far less analgesia. Taking more does not fix it; it just adds side effects.
interactions.what_to_do: A different analgesic is the answer, not a higher codeine dose.

interactions.title: Paracetamol + regular heavy drinking: a narrowed liver margin
interactions.text: Chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1, which is the enzyme that converts paracetamol into the reactive metabolite NAPQI, while heavy drinking also depletes the glutathione that neutralises it. More toxin, less defence. This matters for regular heavy drinking rather than a single evening, and the safe paracetamol dose is genuinely lower.
interactions.what_to_do: Turn on 'regular heavy drinking' in Who's taking it and look at the NAPQI share in the metabolite bar.

interactions.title: Methadone + sedative: a long overlap with a short warning
interactions.text: Methadone's effect fades long before the drug does, so a sedative taken later in the day lands on a methadone level that is still substantial — and methadone accumulates across days. It also prolongs the QT interval. Benzodiazepines are present in a large proportion of methadone deaths.
interactions.what_to_do: Add several days of methadone doses to the timeline and look at where the trough sits before adding anything else.

interactions.title: Two opioids together
interactions.text: Effects on respiration add up regardless of which opioids they are, and tolerance does not transfer neatly between them. Combining a short-acting and a long-acting opioid is especially deceptive, because the short one sets the subjective level while the long one determines how the night ends.
interactions.what_to_do: Treat the total, not each one separately.

interactions.title: Caffeine + smoking: faster caffeine clearance
interactions.text: Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2 and roughly doubles caffeine clearance, which is part of why smokers drink more coffee. The practical consequence comes on quitting: caffeine levels on an unchanged coffee habit rise substantially within about a week, and the resulting jitteriness and insomnia are often mistaken for nicotine withdrawal.
interactions.what_to_do: On quitting smoking, cutting caffeine by roughly a third approximates the old levels.

interactions.title: Methadone + alcohol
interactions.text: Both depress respiration, and methadone's very long half-life means the overlap with an evening's drinking is nearly total. Alcohol also worsens the QT prolongation risk.
interactions.what_to_do: Look at where the methadone trough sits before the drinking starts — it is rarely near zero.

interactions.title: Psychedelic + SSRI: substantially blunted
interactions.text: SSRIs reduce the effect of LSD and psilocybin, usually markedly, through downregulation of the 5-HT2A receptors they act on. This is a pharmacological interaction rather than a dangerous one, but it commonly leads to redosing in pursuit of an effect that is not going to arrive.
interactions.what_to_do: Fluoxetine's metabolite takes weeks to clear, so a recent stop does not remove the blunting.

interactions.title: Psychedelic + stimulant: intensity without stability
interactions.text: Stimulants amplify the anxiety and cardiovascular load of a psychedelic without adding anything to the experience that makes it easier to handle. The combination is associated with a much higher rate of difficult experiences.
interactions.what_to_do: Mostly a psychological risk, and it is the reason a lot of bad experiences happen.
